title: Composition and Surface Termination Control Band Alignments in P3HT/Perovskite Heterostructures
abstract: Hybrid organic-inorganic perovskite heterostructures are emerging platforms for energy conversion and optoelectronic devices, yet the effects of composition and surface terminations on band alignment remain poorly understood. Here, using high-throughput first-principles calculations, we systematically reveal the effect of composition and surface termination on the band alignment of 820 heterostructures formed between poly(3-hexylthiophene) (P3HT) variants and conventional and mixed-cation metal halide perovskites. Band edge analysis predicts concentration dependent band alignments, with most Pb and Sn based perovskites exhibiting Type II and III behavior while mixed-cation CsMASnBr3 uniquely forms Type-I junctions with all P3HT variants. Explicit interface calculations reveal that surface termination can reverse the predicted alignment in conventional tin perovskites, while the mixed cation perovskite preserves Type-I alignment with P3HT regardless of termination. Despite negligible charge transfer, termination dependent band offsets produce markedly different carrier confinement, establishing design principles for engineering P3HT/perovskite interfaces.
summary: This theoretical study uses first-principles calculations to map out how composition and surface termination dictate the band alignment in P3HT/perovskite interfaces. The key finding is that cation mixing in the perovskite structure can stabilize a desirable Type-I junction, and surface termination provides a powerful, tunable knob to engineer carrier confinement for optoelectronic applications.
main_problem: The study aims to understand how the chemical composition and the specific surface termination of metal halide perovskites influence the band alignment at the interface with P3HT organic semiconductors.
main_result: The research found that while most perovskites exhibit Type-II or Type-III band alignments, the mixed-cation $	ext{CsMASnBr}_3$ uniquely forms a Type-I junction, and surface termination can significantly alter the resulting carrier confinement even when charge transfer is negligible.
method: The work relies on high-throughput first-principles calculations, specifically using DFT with advanced functionals like HSE06 and incorporating DFT-D3 corrections for van der Waals interactions.
model_or_system: The system modeled is the heterojunction formed between poly(3-hexylthiophene) (P3HT) variants and various tin-based metal halide perovskites ($	ext{ABX}_3$ and $	ext{AA}'	ext{BX}_3$). The calculations systematically vary the perovskite composition and the nature of the surface termination ($	ext{AX}$ vs. $	ext{BX}$).
key_observables: Band alignment type (Type-I, II, III), band edge positions ($	ext{VBM}$ and $	ext{CBM}$), band offsets ($\Delta	ext{CBM}$, $\Delta	ext{VBM}$), and carrier confinement strength.
important_parameters: Composition of the perovskite (e.g., $	ext{CsSnBr}_3$ vs. $	ext{CsMASnBr}_3$), surface termination ($	ext{AX}$ vs. $	ext{BX}$), and the polymer structure ($	ext{P3HT}$ variants).
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the electronic properties are governed by band offsets and orbital coupling rather than significant net charge transfer, which is confirmed by Bader charge analysis.
figures_summary: Figure 1 compares crystal structures and band edges. Figure 2 is a heatmap summarizing the band-alignment types across 820 heterostructures. Figure 5 details the band alignments and structures for the $	ext{CsMASnBr}_3/	ext{P3HTOM}$ interface under different termination conditions.
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes the influence of composition (comparing pure vs. mixed-cation perovskites) and then details the effect of surface termination on the calculated band alignments, establishing design principles for interface engineering.
why_interesting: Although focused on solid-state photovoltaics, the detailed, first-principles modeling of interfacial electronic structure, band alignment, and charge confinement mechanisms is highly relevant to understanding energy transfer in quantum materials and open quantum systems.
